answer.rationale: Read from durable memory: b1 confirms a release rollback cleared a checkout error spike cleanly with no customer impact, and b6 shows staged gating has caught bad builds before — so a release two hours old is a credible, fast-acting cause for write-path p99 climbing on the primary. b2 shows regional failover works but shifts load and risks write-path complexity during peak settlement. I have capacity for exactly one intervention; rollback is reversible (re-deploy the prior build) and directly addresses the suspected regression without adding load, moving traffic, or shedding writes. I will keep this recommendation guarded: scope the rollback to the suspect build only, keep the prior stable build warm, and avoid conflating with capacity or routing changes. Uncertainties remain — I am not yet certain the release is the cause versus capacity, partner tail-latency, or partial failover — so I will verify the release diff and primary-region error attribution in parallel and be ready to follow up with add_capacity or regional_failover in the next window if rollback does not bend the curve within minutes. I am choosing to spend no verification budget; the rollback decision is well-supported by b1 and b6 even with partial recall, and spending the budget on a memory that wouldn't change the action (e.g., b2's failover details) wastes the only lookup I'm allowed.
